query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration sub-critical annealing (approximately 800–900 °C for 2–4 hours, optionally following moderate cold work) will reduce dislocation pile-ups at lamellar interfaces, thereby alleviating stress concentrations and microcracking, increasing room-temperature tensile ductility by up to ~50–100% relative to the as-cast state, while maintaining or slightly enhancing the baseline ~1 GPa strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase (fcc/B2) hierarchical lamellar microstructure exhibiting limited tensile ductility and brittle fracture at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Short sub-critical annealing (with or without a preceding moderate cold work) to partially coarsen and reconfigure lamellar boundaries without destroying the dual-phase architecture.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing, quasi-static strain rates, and similar testing/operational temperatures up to at least 700 °C where this class of alloys remains structurally stable.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar boundaries and precipitate dispersion formed during sub-critical annealing.
generation.mechanism: Localized stress relaxation at boundaries and reduced propensity for dislocation pile-ups, leading to diminished microcrack nucleation and delayed fracture under applied tension.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significantly improved room-temperature ductility (on the order of 50–100% higher elongation) compared to the as-cast alloy, with strength comparable to or slightly above the baseline ~1 GPa.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar microstructure that exhibits high strength near ~1 GPa but limited room-temperature ductility and early fracture.
generation.boundary: If the annealing temperature is too high or the duration is too long, the lamellar structure may coarsen excessively or degrade, reducing strength. Similarly, insufficient heat treatment time or overly low temperature may not sufficiently reduce local stress concentrations.
generation.uncertainty: Exact annealing parameters (time, temperature) and final microstructural characteristics require fine tuning to balance ductility improvements with retention of strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sample sets from the as-cast alloy: (1) control with no further treatment, (2) moderate cold-roll followed by sub-critical annealing, (3) direct sub-critical annealing without cold work. Perform quantitative microstructural characterization (electron microscopy) before and after treatment, and conduct quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Microstructural changes (lamellar morphology, presence or size of precipitates, dislocation interaction with interfaces)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no measurable reduction in dislocation pile-ups or no improvement in ductility is observed in the treated conditions (2) or (3) versus the as-cast control—even at different sub-critical annealing temperatures or times—then the hypothesis is disproven.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructures (PMC4145285) showed that as-cast lamellae can yield a balance of strength and ductility, but cold working increased strength while sacrificing elongation. Subsequently, researchers working on brittle refractory high-entropy alloys (PMC5995863) demonstrated that a carefully designed thermal treatment could convert a continuous ordered matrix into a more ductile microstructure containing fine precipitates. This partial transformation or precipitation refining reduced dislocation pile-ups at interfaces while retaining high strength. The common thread is that moderate post-casting thermal or thermomechanical steps can break up continuous, brittle phases, refine lamellae, and introduce favorable interfaces that improve ductility without forfeiting strength.
decision.unsolved: Although partial transformation and controlled lamellar refinement have shown promise for improving ductility in brittle EHEAs or refractory HEAs, there remains a need for a concise, single-step process that both alleviates stress concentration at internal boundaries and maintains the hierarchical, plasticity-enhancing microstructure. The best approach to optimize lamellar morphology and minimize dislocation pile-ups remains an open question, particularly for as-cast EHEAs that exhibit limited room-temperature ductility.
decision.lever: A short-duration sub-critical annealing (e.g., ~800–900 °C for 2–4 hours), optionally after moderate cold work, to partially coarsen and reconfigure the lamellar boundaries while preserving the dual-phase architecture.
decision.why: A moderate-temperature annealing step can locally relax stored strain and convert the most brittle, highly ordered interphase boundaries into more ductile interfaces or finely dispersed precipitates. By reducing the propensity for dislocation pile-ups and microcracking at lamellar boundaries, the alloy is expected to gain significant tensile ductility (e.g., an increase of 50–100% in elongation) while retaining or slightly increasing strength (comparable or above the ~1 GPa range). Room-temperature or slightly elevated-temperature mechanical tests (tensile/quasi-static deformation) are ideal to validate this. Prior work (PMC5995863) on B2 + BCC architectures confirmed that converting a continuous ordered phase into a precipitate-dispersed matrix improves ductility, suggesting a similar outcome here. To falsify this hypothesis, one could systematically compare fracture strains, dislocation structures, and interface characteristics among as-cast, cold-worked-then-annealed, and as-cast-then-annealed conditions. Demonstrating that short sub-critical annealing fails to break up the lamellar boundaries and results in no significant ductility improvement would reject the proposed mechanism.
